name: Passiwifi
tagline: Turns WiFi credentials into a scannable QR code plus a printable card guests can use without typing anything.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: WiFi QR codes are a published, open format: a plain text string of the shape WIFI:T:WPA;S:network;P:password;; fed into any QR encoder. There is no server involved, no account needed, and nothing to sync, which means an agent can produce the whole thing as a single static page in well under an hour. The genuine work in a product like this is the polish: nice card templates, print margins that actually line up, hidden-network and WPA3 edge cases, and copy that stops people from pasting their password somewhere public. Your version will be uglier and the print layout will need one round of fighting with CSS. It will also work offline forever and never see your password.
coreLoopDIY: A local static page where you type SSID and password, pick the security type, and get a live QR code plus a print-ready table card, all computed in the browser.
requirements: A QR encoding library, for example the qrcode npm package
A printer if you want the physical card
whatYouLose: Designed card templates that look intentional instead of homemade
Print layout that is already tested against real paper sizes
Edge case handling for hidden networks, WPA3, and passwords containing semicolons or backslashes
A hosted URL you can send to a non-technical person
Any kind of branding or logo upload flow if you run a cafe or rental
moatNotes: The format is a public standard, so the only defensible surface is design quality and the trust that comes from not shipping your WiFi password to a server.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because almost nobody who needs this wants to think about QR payload syntax or CSS print media queries. Airbnb hosts, cafes, and offices want a tidy card in the right size with their logo on it, and they want it in two minutes from a phone. Paying once for a good template beats an afternoon of learning why the printed code scans on an iPhone but not an old Android. That is a real service, it just is not a technical moat.
notes: One of the purest cases on the site: the standard is public, the math is a library call, and the product is the paper it prints on.
prompt:
Build a single-page, fully offline WiFi QR code and guest card generator.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite with vanilla TypeScript, no framework.
- The qrcode npm package for encoding, rendered to a canvas and also to an inline SVG.
- Plain CSS, no Tailwind, no UI kit.
- No backend, no analytics, no fonts loaded from a CDN. Everything must work with the network cable unplugged.

Core behavior:
- Form fields: network name (SSID), password, security type (WPA/WPA2/WPA3, WEP, or none), and a hidden network checkbox.
- Build the payload string as WIFI:T:{type};S:{ssid};P:{password};H:true;; and omit the H segment when the network is not hidden. When security is none, omit the P segment and use T:nopass.
- Escape the characters backslash, semicolon, comma, colon, and double quote in both SSID and password with a leading backslash. Write unit-style assertions for this in a small test file and run them with vitest.
- Re-render the QR code live on every keystroke, debounced 150ms. Use error correction level M, and bump to L automatically if the payload exceeds 200 characters.
- Show the raw payload string in a collapsed details element so the user can see exactly what is encoded.

Card output:
- A printable card area sized for a 4x6 inch index card, plus a second layout sized for a 2x3.5 inch business card.
- Card shows an editable heading (default "Guest WiFi"), the SSID in large monospace text, the password in monospace, and the QR code.
- A print stylesheet that hides the form, sets exact page size, kills margins, and prevents the card from breaking across pages.
- Buttons to download the QR as SVG and as a 1024px PNG.

Explicitly out of scope: accounts, saved networks, cloud storage, logo upload, multi-card sheets, URL sharing of credentials.

Deliverables: working npm run dev, npm run build producing a static dist folder that opens correctly from file:// or any static host, the escaping tests, and a README with one paragraph on why the password never leaves the browser.
